claims.text: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy made from low-activation elements could serve as a structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
Avoiding elements that produce long-lived radionuclides gives the alloy low-activation behavior.
Refractory high-entropy alloys have excellent high-temperature mechanical properties.
High configurational entropy improves radiation tolerance and suppresses defect accumulation relative to monolithic tungsten.
The proposed material is a nanocrystalline solid-solution RHEA with tungsten as its primary matrix element.
Ta, V, or Ti are suitable refractory, low-activation alloying elements for the proposed tungsten matrix.
Fusion plasma-facing materials experience intense helium and neutron bombardment together with high thermal loads.
A temperature of at least 1000 K represents the relevant high-temperature exposure for the proposed plasma-facing material.
Concurrent helium implantation, neutron irradiation, and thermal cycling reproduce relevant fusion plasma-facing conditions.
Stepwise coherent nanoprecipitates form during processing of the proposed alloy.
The high-entropy microstructure and coherent nanoprecipitates inhibit defect nucleation and propagation.
Combining tungsten with selected refractory elements in a high-entropy alloy reduces atomic diffusion under irradiation.
Combining tungsten with selected refractory elements in a high-entropy alloy reduces irradiation-induced defect mobility.
Coherent interfaces or nanoprecipitates act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
Low-activation alloy chemistry minimizes the formation of long-lived radionuclides.
The proposed tungsten-based RHEA will produce fewer long-lived activation products than pure tungsten under simulated fusion conditions.
The proposed tungsten-based RHEA will retain better high-temperature mechanical performance than pure tungsten.
The proposed tungsten-based RHEA will resist helium-induced surface degradation better than pure tungsten.
Tungsten is currently a material of choice for fusion tokamak plasma-facing applications.
Current pure tungsten and tungsten-based plasma-facing materials suffer from helium bubble formation and high activation under irradiation.
